questions.prompt: To merge overlapping intervals, the essential first step is to:

options.text: Sort the intervals by their start point
Put them in a hash set
Reverse the list
Sort the intervals by their length

questions.explanation: Once sorted by start, a single pass can extend or close the current merged interval, since any overlap must involve an adjacent interval. This makes the whole process O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Two intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap when:

options.text: b < c
a <= d and c <= b
b == d
a == c

questions.explanation: They overlap unless one ends before the other begins, which the condition a <= d and c <= b captures. It is often easier to test the non-overlap case and negate it.

questions.prompt: The minimum number of meeting rooms needed for a set of intervals can be found by:

options.text: A hash map of room numbers
A min-heap of end times, or a sweep line over sorted start and end events
Sorting by length and counting
A single linear scan without sorting

questions.explanation: Processing starts and ends in time order, the peak number of simultaneously active meetings is the answer. A min-heap of end times reuses a room whenever the earliest meeting has finished.

questions.prompt: To select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, the greedy rule is to sort by:

options.text: Length, taking the shortest
Start time, taking the earliest start
End time, then repeatedly take the earliest-finishing compatible interval
Start time, taking the latest start

questions.explanation: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for later intervals, which an exchange argument proves optimal. This is the activity-selection problem.

questions.prompt: The sweep-line technique processes geometric or interval events by:

options.text: Randomly sampling points
Building a hash table of coordinates
Sorting all endpoints and moving a conceptual line across them, updating an active set
Recursing on the midpoint

questions.explanation: Sorting events and advancing a line lets you maintain the set of currently active intervals or segments, answering overlap and counting questions efficiently. It is fundamental in computational geometry.

questions.prompt: Custom sorting a list of objects by a computed key is typically done by:

options.text: Providing a comparator or key function to a standard O(n log n) sort
Writing a new bubble sort each time
Reversing the list
Hashing the objects

questions.explanation: Library sorts accept a comparator or key selector, so any ordering is expressed without reimplementing the algorithm. The underlying sort remains O(n log n).

questions.prompt: When is a stable sort specifically required?

options.text: When all keys are distinct
When the array is already sorted
When memory is unlimited
When sorting by a secondary key must preserve the order established by a previous sort on a primary key

questions.explanation: Stability keeps equal keys in their prior relative order, which lets multi-key sorting be done one key at a time. With distinct keys, stability makes no observable difference.

questions.prompt: To find whether any two of a set of intervals overlap, the most efficient approach is to:

options.text: Build a binary search tree keyed on length
Store them in a hash set
Compare every pair of intervals
Sort by start and check each interval against the previous one

questions.explanation: After sorting by start, an overlap can only occur between consecutive intervals, so a single linear scan suffices. This is O(n log n) versus the O(n^2) of checking all pairs.

questions.prompt: The insert-interval problem (add a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list and merge) runs in:

options.text: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)

questions.explanation: Since the list is already sorted, one linear pass places the new interval and merges any it overlaps. No re-sorting is needed, so it is linear rather than O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Many interval problems reduce to sorting because sorting:

options.text: Brings related intervals adjacent, so a linear scan can decide overlaps locally
Guarantees O(1) total time
Removes all duplicates
Converts intervals into a hash table

questions.explanation: Ordering by an endpoint means any interaction happens between neighbours, replacing global pairwise checks with a local sweep. This is why sorting is the first move in most interval algorithms.
